title: Hygiene for makeup application: shared products, applicators and tools
audience: Makeup artists who apply makeup to more than one client, and who share product pots, brushes, sponges and other tools
learningOutcomes: Explain how makeup application can spread infection between clients
Take product from a shared container without contaminating it or passing contamination to the next client
Name the Victorian guideline that applies to make-up application, and the parts of it this draft has not yet confirmed
referencesAtStart: Official references for this lesson: Department of Health Victoria, Hairdressing and make-up application: infection prevention and control (updated 19 August 2019); Department of Health Victoria, Health guidelines for personal care and body art industries (updated 26 October 2026); WA Department of Health, Advice for the beauty therapy industry (last reviewed 15 April 2021). The WA page is a different state's guidance and is used here as practice guidance only.

instruction.heading: Why makeup application needs an infection control plan
instruction.body: The Victorian Department of Health states that make-up application can transmit infection. Product pots, pencils, brushes and sponges move from one client's face to the next, and a contaminated product can carry an infection from one person to another. Hygiene for makeup work is therefore a planned routine, not a one-off clean at the end of the day. The plan covers how product is taken from a container, which tools are single-use, which are cleaned and disinfected between clients, and how the kit is stored and transported between bookings.

instruction.heading: The governing guideline for Victoria
instruction.body: The Victorian Department of Health states that hairdressing and temporary make-up application businesses must follow the Infection prevention and control guidelines for hair, beauty, tattooing and skin penetration industries (2019). That guideline is the source for the detailed rules on cleaning, disinfection and single-use items in Victoria. The text of that guideline was not read for this draft. The specific rules on make-up applicators, shared pots and reusable tools are therefore UNCONFIRMED here, and the lesson must not be approved until a reviewer has read the guideline and checked the rules below against it.

instruction.heading: Taking product from a shared container
instruction.body: The WA Department of Health advises that product in a tub, such as makeup, powder or cream, is removed from stock with a clean single-use applicator. The same guidance says that applicator must not be used on another client, and must not be dipped back into the original container. Leftover product is discarded rather than returned to the container. The WA page is practice guidance from another state. This course adopts the approach as the minimum standard for shared pots until the Victorian guideline is confirmed. The rule does not change for a pot the artist owns, because the next client is still at risk.

instruction.heading: Tools that are reused
instruction.body: Where a tool is reused, it is cleaned and disinfected between clients, using the method the governing guideline sets. The WA guidance states that reusable containers must be cleaned and disinfected between clients. Which brushes, sponges and other applicators may be reused, and which must be single-use, is UNCONFIRMED in this draft. A business chooses a single-use or a disinfect-and-dry approach for each tool on its kit, writes the choice on the approved kit list, and applies it at every appointment. A tool that has touched broken skin, blood or another body fluid is not reused on any client.

procedure: Check the governing guideline for the tool type before setting the kit list, and record the source
Take product from any shared pot or tub with a clean single-use applicator, never with a brush or fingers that have touched the client
Discard leftover product from the applicator, and do not return it to the container
Clean and disinfect each reusable tool between clients, using the method in the guideline, and let it dry before storage
Place used single-use items directly into a lidded waste container at the appointment
Record the kit check and the cleaning routine at the start and end of each day or booking run

workedExamples.situation: A makeup artist dips a clean brush into a shared lipstick pot, then uses the same brush on the next client without cleaning.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is wrong, and what should happen instead?
workedExamples.reasoning: The brush carries product and anything on it from one client to the next, and the shared pot is contaminated. The artist must take product with a clean single-use applicator, not a brush that has been used on a client. The brush must be cleaned and disinfected or discarded according to the approved kit list before the next client.

workedExamples.situation: A client asks for a product from the artist's own pot to be applied with a fingertip, to save time.
workedExamples.reasoning: A fingertip carries the risk of spreading infection from the product pot. The artist applies the product with a single-use applicator, or offers a single-dose product, and records the method. Ownership of the pot does not change the risk to the next client.

equipmentAndPpe: Clean single-use applicators for taking product from shared pots
Disinfectant and cleaning materials approved in the governing guideline for the reusable tools on the kit
Lidded waste container for single-use items
Gloves for handling tools and products, changed between clients

commonErrors.error: Dipping a used brush or sponge back into a shared pot.
commonErrors.prevention: Take product with a clean single-use applicator, and never return used tools to a pot.

commonErrors.error: Returning leftover product to the original container.
commonErrors.prevention: Discard leftover product from the applicator. Do not return it to the pot.

commonErrors.error: Assuming an artist's own product pot is safe to share without a routine.
commonErrors.prevention: Apply the same routine to every pot, because the next client is still at risk.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: The Victorian Department of Health states that make-up application can transmit infection, and that temporary make-up application businesses must follow the 2019 infection prevention and control guideline for hair, beauty, tattooing and skin penetration industries.

UNCONFIRMED: the Victorian guideline's specific rules for make-up applicators, shared pots, and cleaning or disinfection of reusable tools. These must be read in the guideline before this lesson is approved.
The WA guidance on single-use applicators for shared pots is from another state and is used as practice guidance only. It does not set a Victorian or national requirement.

qualityStandard: Product is taken from every shared container with a clean single-use applicator
No used tool is returned to a shared container
Each reusable tool on the kit has a recorded cleaning method, taken from the governing guideline
documentationEvidence: Approved kit list showing single-use and reusable tools, with the source for each rule
Cleaning and disinfection record for reusable tools, by booking or by day
Record of a kit check, and of any tool removed from use
summary: Make-up application can transmit infection, so hygiene is a planned routine
Victoria's governing guideline is the 2019 infection prevention and control guideline for hair, beauty, tattooing and skin penetration industries
Product is taken from shared pots with a clean single-use applicator, and leftovers are discarded
The specific tool rules are UNCONFIRMED until the Victorian guideline is read

knowledgeChecks.question: What should be used to take product from a shared pot?
options: The brush used on the previous client
A fingertip from the same hand used on the client's face

knowledgeChecks.question: A little product is left on the applicator after a client. Where does it go?
options: Back into the shared pot, so nothing is wasted
Onto the next client's skin to finish the look
Into the bin or waste container, not back into the pot

knowledgeChecks.question: Which document does the Victorian Department of Health say make-up application businesses must follow?
options: The Infection prevention and control guidelines for hair, beauty, tattooing and skin penetration industries (2019)
No document, because make-up does not break the skin
